newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem workers return to disputed border village.
newsitem.headline: Moslem workers return to disputed border village.

text.p: Moslem construction workers safely entered a village on the Serb side of Bosnia's ethnic boundary line on Thursday five days after they were attacked by a Serb mob.

A Reuters reporter saw up to 30 Moslems in the northeastern Gajevi village, erecting pre-fabricated houses that would temporarily accommodate other Moslems who are expected to resettle the half-destroyed village in the next few weeks.
"The situation is quiet and we feel like working so I expect we shall move the first families back in by February 10," village leader Hadzib Mehikic said.
A mob of up to 100 Serbs armed with crowbars assaulted Moslems delivering construction material to Gajevi over the weekend and injured at least three of them.
The NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) and international officials expressed outrage over the attack and demanded Serb authorities guarantee the safety of the returnees.

Under the Dayton peace treaty, which halted the 43-month long Bosnian war in December 1995, refugees are guaranteed the right to move back to their homes but ethnic mistrust and nationalist policies of Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders have hindered the return so far.
Bosnian Serb militia overran the region at the outset of war in 1992 and expelled non-Serb residents in a bid to carve out a separate state.

Carl Bildt, international High Representative to Bosnia, has met Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic twice since the Gajevi incident, demanding assurances that Serb police would allow Moslems to return and supervise the process.
A vetting procedure supervised by international agencies granted permission to 36 Moslem families to move back to Gajevi after they proved their pre-war residency.
But Plavsic indicated on Thursday that she disagreed with the results of the vetting procedure, alleging only six families had the right to move back, the Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA reported.

The Serb political leadership opposed Bosnia's break from Serbian-dominated Yugoslavia and has resisted efforts to allow Moslems and Croats to move back to their pre-war homes in Serb-controlled territory.

SFOR Captain Chuck Sullivan said on Thursday that Serbs and international police monitors were jointly patrolling the Gajevi area and U.S. and Russian soldiers with SFOR were deployed to prevent possible bloodshed.

"We are here to keep the...Serbs and Moslems apart. We're not here to protect houses but we won't let atrocities occur," Sullivan told reporters. "We won't stand by and watch Moslems or Serbs get beaten up."
